title: Don't Ditch That Textbook
author: Sol in the Wild
summary: The author of 'Sol in the Wild' pushes back on the 'Ditch That Textbook' movement and its ideological descendants -- gamified lessons, digital scavenger hunts, AI-generated activities, and Instagram-style templates -- arguing that these approaches confuse engagement with entertainment and complexity with rigour. The article contends that simple, cognitively demanding practices (teacher explanation, student writing, retrieval practice, structured discussion) align with how learning actually works, while over-designed instruction competes for the limited attention and working memory that learning itself requires. Students, the author argues, are acute detectors of performative learning versus authentic intellectual work; classrooms centred on thinking rather than performance are more, not less, authentic to them.
points: Over-designed instruction -- decorative slides, multi-app workflows, gamified 'fun' layers -- competes for limited working memory and attention, adding extrinsic load without supporting the cognitive work that constitutes learning.

The revolution education needs is not more elaborate disguises for learning but a rediscovery of the power of simply teaching well: explanation, writing, retrieval practice, discussion, and reflection.

Students can distinguish between authentic intellectual work and performative engagement; classrooms chasing social-media aesthetics signal to students that adults are trying too hard rather than trusting the inherent demands of the content.
Simple is not simplistic -- 'simple is often cognitively superior' because it keeps attention on the knowledge itself rather than on navigating the activity's mechanics.

Practices such as quiet writing, teacher modelling, partner discussion, mini-whiteboard responses, and spaced retrieval may look ordinary but 'work because they align with how learning actually happens.'
quotes: Students can tell the difference between authentic intellectual work and performative engagement. One feels real. The other feels forced. Students are incredibly good at detecting when adults are trying too hard.

Every decorative slide, complicated procedure, multiple-app workflow, or 'fun' layer students must navigate competes for limited attention and working memory. Instead of supporting thinking, it can overload it.
Simple is not simplistic. Simple is often cognitively superior.

Not every lesson needs to feel like a game show. Not every activity needs to mimic TikTok. Not every classroom task needs a gimmick attached to it to justify its existence. More often than not, students simply need to quietly grapple with important ideas.

There is something deeply authentic about classrooms centered on thinking rather than performance. A room where students are actively wrestling with knowledge instead of constantly consuming polished to resemble 'their world' activities designed to keep them superficially entertained.
The revolution we need in education is not finding increasingly elaborate ways to disguise learning. It is rediscovering the power of simply teaching well.
